items.title: 4.1 Differential equations: Definition, Order and Degree

source_refs.note: Book p. 124: Unit 4 introduction, 4.1 definition of a differential equation, six example equations (sixth printed '(iv)'), order and degree

blocks.text: The idea of differential equations was first proposed by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz during the development of calculus. The term "differential equation" was introduced by Leibniz in 1676. In the 18th century, mathematicians like Euler and Lagrange made significant contributions to the theory of these equations. Over the centuries, research by hundreds of mathematicians, physicists, economists, chemists and other scientists around the world has broadened the range of applications and the methods to solve differential equations.

For example, if a particle covers a distance \(s\) in time \(t\), then its velocity \(v\) and acceleration \(a\) can be represented by the differential equations
\[v = \dfrac{ds}{dt}\]
\[a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\]
To begin our study of this important topic, we first define a differential equation and classify its various types.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Recall from Grade XI: a derivative is a rate of change. \(\frac{ds}{dt}\) tells how fast the distance changes with time, i.e. the velocity, and \(\frac{dv}{dt}\) tells how fast the velocity changes, i.e. the acceleration. A differential equation is simply an equation that contains such a rate. In real life we usually know how fast something changes (a rate) before we know the quantity itself, so the laws of physics, biology and economics are naturally written as differential equations. Solving the equation then gives the quantity itself.

An equation that involves at least one derivative of a dependent variable with respect to an independent variable is called a differential equation, and in particular it is called an ordinary differential equation. For example:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), \(x\) is the independent variable (we choose it freely) and \(y\) is the dependent variable (its value depends on \(x\)). "Ordinary" means there is only one independent variable, so only ordinary derivatives such as \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) appear. (Equations with several independent variables and partial derivatives are studied in higher classes.) An equation like \(y = x^{2} + 1\) is not a differential equation, because no derivative appears in it.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book labels the sixth equation "(iv)" a second time. It should be (vi):
\[\text{(vi)}\quad \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\]
In the next paragraph, "equation (iv) has order 3" refers to the first (iv), \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 1 = \cos\left(\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\right)\). The sixth equation (vi) has order 2.

The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative that appears in the differential equation. For example, the order of the equations (i) and (v) is 1, the order of equations (ii) and (iii) is 2, whereas equation (iv) has order 3. A differential equation of order 1 is called a first-order differential equation, such as (i) and (v).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How to read the order: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is the first derivative (order 1), \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) is the second derivative (order 2), \(\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\) is the third (order 3). The small number on top of \(d\) and on \(dx\) is the order of that derivative; it is NOT a power. Look at every derivative in the equation and take the largest such number. In (iv) the third derivative sits inside a cosine, but it is still there, so the order is 3. The sixth equation (vi) contains \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), so its order is 2.

The degree of a differential equation is the greatest exponent of the highest-order derivative appearing in the differential equation. For example, differential equation (v) is a polynomial in \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), and its degree is 2.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The degree only makes sense when the equation is (or can be made) a polynomial in all its derivatives. So:
1. First clear any root or fractional power that contains a derivative (isolate it and raise both sides to a suitable power).
2. If a derivative is stuck inside sin, cos, log, an exponential, etc., the degree is not defined (no algebra can remove it). The order is still defined.
3. Then the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative only. Powers of \(x\), \(y\) or of lower derivatives do not count.
In (v), \(\sqrt{xy}\) is only a function of \(x\) and \(y\), not of a derivative, so it does not disturb the degree; the highest derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) appears squared, so the degree is 2.

blocks.caption: Our summary of the six example equations (not printed in the book); here \(y' = \frac{dy}{dx}\), \(y'' = \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\), \(y''' = \frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}\)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Answer order and degree questions in three short lines: (1) name the highest derivative, so the order; (2) say whether any derivative is inside a function like sin or e, or under a root; (3) clear roots if needed and read the power of the highest derivative, so the degree. Writing these three lines earns full marks even when the answer is "degree not defined".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A differential equation contains at least one derivative of a dependent variable with respect to an independent variable; with one independent variable it is an ordinary differential equation.
2. Order = order of the highest derivative present.
3. Degree = power of that highest derivative, after the equation is written as a polynomial in its derivatives.
4. If a derivative is inside sin, cos, log, \(e^{(\ )}\), etc., the degree is not defined.
5. First-order differential equations (order 1) are the subject of this unit.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the largest power anywhere as the degree: in \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{5} = 0\) the degree is 1, not 5, because only the power of the highest derivative counts.
2. Reading the "2" in \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) as a power: it is the order of the derivative.
3. Reading the degree before clearing a root: \(\sqrt{\frac{dy}{dx}} = \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\) has degree 2 (square both sides), not 1.
4. Confusing \(e^{y}\) or \(\sin y\) (functions of \(y\), harmless) with \(e^{dy/dx}\) or \(\sin\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\) (derivative inside a function, degree not defined).
